title: Single-frame narrative compression and inferable event structure
limitations: The empirical evidence is strongest for picture stories and event comprehension, not isolated commercial key art.
A single frame cannot guarantee that every viewer infers the same missing event.
Genre literacy and reading direction can change which clues are noticed first.
reuse_note: Use these mechanisms as causal staging atoms for original scenes; do not copy a cited artwork, character, or franchise composition.

mechanisms.statement: Place a legible actor, action, target, and spatiotemporal anchor so the viewer can establish an event model within the first inspection.
Let a visible action carry the narrative before relying on lore labels, decorative insignia, or explanatory text.
Omit one intermediate causal step only when the frame preserves both a readable prior-state clue and a readable consequence clue.
Limit simultaneous coherence gaps because several missing links split the event into competing explanations instead of one productive inference.
Stage the subject at a temporal boundary where posture, object state, and environmental reaction jointly indicate what has just changed or is about to change.
For a pre-event moment, expose the intended target and a directional vector so anticipation has a concrete possible consequence.
For an aftermath moment, retain residue, displacement, damage, repair, or witness response that points back to a plausible cause.
Keep the central causal chain inferable while leaving one peripheral motive, source, or outcome unresolved for rereading.

illustration_evidence_definitions.actor_action_target_triangle: The actor, performed action, and affected target are all visually locatable.
illustration_evidence_definitions.causal_state_change: At least one object, body, or environment element visibly differs from its implied prior state.
illustration_evidence_definitions.consequence_trace: Residue or response makes the action consequential rather than merely posed.
illustration_evidence_definitions.temporal_boundary_pose: The pose is caught during commitment, interruption, impact, release, or recovery rather than neutral display.
illustration_evidence_definitions.bridging_gap_cue: A deliberately omitted step is bracketed by enough evidence to support a specific inference.
illustration_evidence_definitions.off_frame_cause_vector: Gaze, motion, light, debris, or sound reaction indicates a relevant cause outside the crop.
illustration_evidence_definitions.setting_time_anchor: Weather, light, clock-like state, wear, or activity establishes when and where the event is happening.
illustration_evidence_definitions.narrative_ambiguity_budget: Only one major narrative variable is intentionally unresolved while the main action remains legible.

candidate_definitions.actor_action_target_triangle: Compose an original actor-action-target relationship that survives thumbnail inspection.
candidate_definitions.causal_state_change: Specify one visible before-to-after change caused inside the scene.
candidate_definitions.consequence_trace: Add one material or social trace that proves the action mattered.
candidate_definitions.temporal_boundary_pose: Choose commitment, interruption, impact, release, or recovery as the captured instant.
candidate_definitions.bridging_gap_cue: Remove exactly one causal step while retaining its input and output evidence.
candidate_definitions.off_frame_cause_vector: Point one readable visual vector toward a meaningful off-frame cause.
candidate_definitions.setting_time_anchor: Bind the event to a concrete place-and-time condition through visible evidence.
candidate_definitions.narrative_ambiguity_budget: Reserve ambiguity for one secondary question, not for the core action.

compatibility: Combines with relationship blocking when each participant has a distinct causal role.
Combines with recurring motifs when a motif visibly changes state because of the event.
Combines with gesture flow when pose and environmental reaction share the same force direction.
Combines with environmental storytelling when background traces support the same event chain.
Combines with crop-resilient key art when the actor-action-target triangle remains inside the safe area.
conflicts: Conflicts with exposition that must be read before the action can be understood.
Conflicts with several equal-intensity climaxes competing in one frame.
Conflicts with unrelated decorative props that imply additional unsupported plots.
Conflicts with a fully resolved tableau that leaves no causal question or discovery.
Conflicts with atmospheric effects that obscure the target or consequence.
counterexamples: A polished character portrait with no affected target or state change.
A dynamic attack pose whose target, risk, and consequence are absent.
A ruined city filled with random debris that cannot be attributed to any visible event.
A frame whose mystery depends only on hidden lore named in a caption.
A reaction shot where every surrounding clue points to a different off-frame cause.
boundaries: Do not treat a single-frame illustration as a substitute for multi-panel pacing grammar.
Do not require generated text, interface labels, or lore captions for comprehension.
Do not reuse protected characters, signature props, or recognizable franchise compositions.
Do not infer personality, morality, nationality, or diagnosis from pose or damage cues.
Do not increase violence or distress merely to manufacture narrative stakes.
format_implications: For covers, preserve the causal triangle outside title-safe space.
For cards, choose one state change that remains readable inside the frame mask.
For banners, use an off-frame vector without cropping away its origin.
For vertical key art, stack cause, actor, and consequence along a single readable axis.
viewer_implications: The first pass should answer who is doing what to which target.
The second pass should reveal a prior-state or consequence trace.
The frame should invite one bridge inference rather than demand background knowledge.
Uncertainty should deepen motive or outcome without obscuring the core event.

title: The Scene Perception & Event Comprehension Theory Applied to Visual Narratives
supported_dimensions: Early fixations establish who, what, where, and when for an event model.
People and their actions are strong candidates for the foundation of visual event comprehension.
Incoming visual information and stored event knowledge jointly guide attention.
limitations: The article synthesizes a research program rather than testing one isolated illustration prompt system.
Much of the evidence concerns sequential static images and film.
Attention findings are probabilistic and do not prescribe a universal scan path.
reuse_note: Abstract event-model requirements and predictive-inference cues only; do not reproduce any study stimulus or named narrative property.

title: Bridging a Gap in Coherence: The Coordination of Comprehension Processes When Viewing Visual Narratives
supported_dimensions: Removing a bridging action increases both segmentation and explanation generation.
Viewers can generate an inference to close a coherence gap.
Mapping and shifting responses depend on whether bridging evidence is present.
limitations: The experiments used wordless picture-story episodes rather than standalone key art.
A productive omission in a sequence does not establish the optimal ambiguity level for every genre.
Think-aloud explanations may not capture all implicit interpretations.
reuse_note: Use the demonstrated gap-and-bridge relationship to bound omission; do not assume that more missing information always improves engagement.

title: Focal routing and layered attention hierarchy
limitations: Eye tracking on paintings does not directly predict attention for every illustration genre or device size.
Focal points are more reliable than an exact intended fixation order.
Prior knowledge, task, culture, and display context change gaze behavior.
reuse_note: Use attention mechanisms as probabilistic composition controls and verify rendered output at target size; never claim deterministic gaze capture.

mechanisms.statement: Create one primary focal anchor by co-locating semantic importance with a local contrast, clarity, or isolation difference.
Use large-scale composition to guide the first inspection, when spatial structure has stronger leverage than it does during prolonged viewing.
Treat leading lines and compositional paths as probabilistic invitations because viewers often reach focal points without following the intended sequence exactly.
Reserve the sharpest edge or finest resolution for a meaningful area instead of distributing equal finish across the frame.
Balance competing color patches, line density, and intersections so no incidental region overwhelms the intended subject.
Pair low-level salience with story relevance because contrast can attract attention without explaining why the region matters.
Give a secondary discovery node a weaker but distinct contrast signature linked back to the primary focal anchor.
Arrange gesture, gaze, repeated shape, or value transitions so peripheral exploration has a plausible route back to the primary subject.

illustration_evidence_definitions.primary_focal_anchor: One region clearly carries the principal narrative or character information.
illustration_evidence_definitions.first_fixation_contrast: The primary region has a measurable relative difference in value, chroma, size, isolation, or clarity.
illustration_evidence_definitions.secondary_discovery_node: A subordinate region rewards continued viewing without competing with the primary anchor.
illustration_evidence_definitions.guiding_vector_chain: Two or more directional cues point toward related information rather than decorative dead ends.
illustration_evidence_definitions.edge_sharpness_gradient: Edge precision decreases away from the intended area of inspection.
illustration_evidence_definitions.contrast_isolation: The highest local contrast is spatially contained instead of repeated everywhere.
illustration_evidence_definitions.semantic_relevance_anchor: The visually prominent element is also causally or relationally important to the scene.
illustration_evidence_definitions.scanpath_return_cue: A peripheral cue redirects gaze toward the primary subject through gaze, gesture, repetition, or value transition.

candidate_definitions.primary_focal_anchor: Name the single most important visible region before adding supporting detail.
candidate_definitions.first_fixation_contrast: Assign that region one dominant relative contrast mechanism.
candidate_definitions.secondary_discovery_node: Add one lower-priority discovery that explains or complicates the primary subject.
candidate_definitions.guiding_vector_chain: Connect at least two directional cues to meaningful destinations.
candidate_definitions.edge_sharpness_gradient: Concentrate fine edges near the primary region and simplify elsewhere.
candidate_definitions.contrast_isolation: Prevent the maximum contrast pattern from repeating in unrelated regions.
candidate_definitions.semantic_relevance_anchor: Require the focal element to affect the story, relationship, or action.
candidate_definitions.scanpath_return_cue: Use one peripheral repetition or gesture to bring attention back to the principal subject.

compatibility: Combines with value grouping when the focal anchor occupies a distinct value band.
Combines with gesture flow when limbs, fabric, and effects point to the same semantic target.
Combines with motif systems when repeated motifs diminish away from the primary anchor.
Combines with environmental storytelling when secondary clues form a controlled discovery path.
Combines with crop resilience when the hierarchy survives every required aspect ratio.
conflicts: Conflicts with equal sharpness and equal contrast across the entire image.
Conflicts with decorative leading lines that terminate at empty or irrelevant regions.
Conflicts with a visually dominant face or effect that has no narrative relevance.
Conflicts with several competing primary subjects of equal scale and salience.
Conflicts with center placement used as the only evidence of hierarchy.
counterexamples: A highly detailed image where every accessory has the same edge precision.
A bright effect in a corner that pulls attention away from the actual action.
A road or weapon that points out of frame without a meaningful off-frame cause.
A centered character surrounded by equally saturated signage and particles.
A composition that works full-size but loses its focal subject at thumbnail scale.
boundaries: Do not promise an exact universal scan path from composition alone.
Do not infer viewer interest, intelligence, personality, or culture from fixation order.
Do not depend only on hue contrast; retain value and shape separation for varied color vision.
Do not copy a protected key-art layout or signature composition.
Do not use attention control to conceal required commercial or safety information.
format_implications: At thumbnail scale, preserve the primary mass and one contrast mechanism.
For covers, keep title-safe space from becoming a second focal anchor.
For cards, verify that the frame and effects do not sever guiding vectors.
For banners, rebuild the hierarchy for the crop rather than merely trimming the original.
viewer_implications: Most viewers should find the primary subject quickly without needing identical fixation order.
Continued inspection should reveal one causally relevant secondary node.
Peripheral detail should support return or progression rather than trap attention.
The hierarchy should remain legible under different prior knowledge and viewing duration.

title: The role that composition plays in determining how a viewer looks at landscape art
supported_dimensions: Known focal points attracted and held attention in the tested works.
Spatial features guided short-duration viewing more consistently than longer viewing.
The intended entry, exit, and exact path were less reliable than focal attraction.
limitations: The analyzed subset was small and concentrated on landscape paintings.
Central placement can confound an intended focal-point effect.
Five-second laboratory viewing differs from mobile browsing and commercial selection.
reuse_note: Use focal attraction and early composition findings, while preserving scanpath uncertainty and testing the actual output format.

title: How Do We See Art: An Eye-Tracker Study
supported_dimensions: A localized sharpness manipulation produced a common attention pattern.
Changing color patches and line-density relationships altered visual balance.
Low-level salience and higher-level experience jointly contributed to gaze variability.
limitations: The stimulus set and participant sample were limited.
Fixation counts do not alone establish narrative comprehension or preference.
Results from specific art manipulations should not be generalized into rigid layout rules.
reuse_note: Translate the reported manipulations into relative edge, contrast, and density controls rather than copying any source image arrangement.

title: Silhouette, contour structure, and non-essentialist shape language
limitations: Object-recognition studies use controlled objects rather than expressive character casts.
Silhouette readability does not prove emotional meaning, personality, or cultural identity.
A canonical view may overstate recognizability that fails under pose or crop changes.
reuse_note: Use contour and part-structure mechanisms to create original readable designs; never map basic shapes to human worth, personality, diagnosis, gender, ethnicity, or nationality.

mechanisms.statement: Use the outer contour for coarse category and cast separation, but do not rely on it as the sole carrier of identity.
Preserve a small set of internal part boundaries that clarify how masses connect and distinguish closely related designs.
Place informative concavities and curvature changes at functional joints or attachment boundaries rather than adding arbitrary spikes.
Test recognizability across canonical and noncanonical views because a strong single silhouette can conceal weak three-dimensional structure.
Differentiate a cast through proportion, appendage placement, negative space, and mass rhythm without assigning personality or morality to a geometric primitive.
Pair an economical outer silhouette with internal contour or shading cues when the design must communicate depth and construction.
Keep a few landmark ratios stable across poses while allowing gesture-dependent changes in the overall contour.
Judge silhouette and internal boundaries at the final display size and against the intended background rather than only on a white design sheet.

illustration_evidence_definitions.thumbnail_outer_contour: The subject remains separable as one coherent mass at intended thumbnail size.
illustration_evidence_definitions.internal_part_boundary: A limited internal contour clarifies a joint, overlap, or construction change.
illustration_evidence_definitions.concavity_landmark: A meaningful inward turn marks a part boundary or functional attachment.
illustration_evidence_definitions.cast_shape_contrast: Multiple characters differ in mass distribution and spacing without stereotype labels.
illustration_evidence_definitions.negative_space_window: Open spaces between limbs, costume, props, or body masses preserve pose readability.
illustration_evidence_definitions.pose_invariant_landmarks: Selected proportion and attachment landmarks survive pose and costume changes.
illustration_evidence_definitions.multi_view_recognition: The design remains identifiable from more than one view or action state.
illustration_evidence_definitions.background_figure_separation: The contour remains readable against the actual background value and texture.

candidate_definitions.thumbnail_outer_contour: Specify a coarse outer mass that survives reduction without accessory detail.
candidate_definitions.internal_part_boundary: Add only the internal boundaries needed to explain construction or identity.
candidate_definitions.concavity_landmark: Use a functional concavity at one important joint or attachment.
candidate_definitions.cast_shape_contrast: Separate cast members through proportions, spacing, and mass rhythm without personality coding.
candidate_definitions.negative_space_window: Preserve at least one clear negative-space opening around the action.
candidate_definitions.pose_invariant_landmarks: Name two or three stable ratios or attachment positions for identity continuity.
candidate_definitions.multi_view_recognition: Check the same design in at least two materially different orientations.
candidate_definitions.background_figure_separation: Set contour, rim, or value separation for the actual environment.

compatibility: Combines with gesture flow when stable landmarks coexist with pose-specific contour deformation.
Combines with costume-state design when layers preserve the core mass and selected negative spaces.
Combines with focal routing when the clearest contour belongs to the narrative anchor.
Combines with creature ecology when appendages have functional attachment and movement logic.
Combines with sequential continuity when invariant landmarks are documented across states.
conflicts: Conflicts with assigning moral or personality traits to circles, squares, triangles, or body proportions.
Conflicts with copying a protected character's recognizable silhouette or signature accessory arrangement.
Conflicts with accessory accumulation that closes every negative-space window.
Conflicts with a design recognizable only from one staged pose.
Conflicts with an outer silhouette that contradicts internal joint and depth structure.
counterexamples: A black shape readable only because it duplicates a famous protected outline.
Three cast members with different colors but identical mass distribution and appendage spacing.
A spiked contour whose points do not correspond to anatomy, tools, clothing, or motion.
A side view that reads clearly while front and action views collapse into an undifferentiated mass.
A silhouette test that passes on white but disappears against the production background.
boundaries: Never infer or prescribe personality, morality, emotion, gender, ethnicity, nationality, or diagnosis from basic shape alone.
Do not treat external silhouette as sufficient evidence of three-dimensional construction.
Do not imitate protected character outlines, signature costumes, or identifiable prop constellations.
Do not generalize human perception findings directly to every image-generation model.
Do not maximize distinctiveness through demeaning or culturally coded bodily exaggeration.
format_implications: For thumbnails, prioritize the outer mass and one negative-space window.
For cards, ensure borders and effects do not erase appendage or pose landmarks.
For turnarounds, preserve attachment points and mass ratios across views.
For ensemble key art, separate overlapping characters with alternating contours and value gaps.
viewer_implications: Viewers should distinguish the subject before reading surface texture or costume detail.
Closer viewing should reveal internal construction that supports rather than contradicts the silhouette.
Cast differentiation should remain descriptive and functional, not essentialist.
Recognition should persist across pose, crop, and background changes.

title: Shape Information Mediating Basic- and Subordinate-Level Object Recognition Revealed by Analyses of Eye Movements
supported_dimensions: Observers preferentially fixated part boundaries during both basic and subordinate classification.
Concave bounding-contour regions received more fixation than convex regions.
Internal boundaries and curvature polarity carried functional shape information.
limitations: The study used novel controlled objects rather than characters or expressive illustrations.
Fixation preference does not authorize semantic personality interpretation.
Results concern recognition tasks and may differ under free aesthetic viewing.
reuse_note: Use part-boundary and curvature findings for readable construction; prohibit emotional or demographic labeling of shapes.

title: Learning the 3-D structure of objects from 2-D views depends on shape, not format
supported_dimensions: Silhouette training improved recognition but underperformed line, shading, and stereo formats for robust three-dimensional learning.
Internal and external shape information supported generalization to novel views.
Familiarity, canonical view, and available features affect silhouette recognition.
limitations: The task used novel nonliving objects and intensive laboratory training.
The findings do not establish an ideal level of stylization for character art.
Recognition performance cannot by itself measure appeal or originality.
reuse_note: Use silhouette as a coarse check and add internal structural cues for multiview identity; do not equate recognition with artistic quality.

title: Value grouping, palette roles, and context-sensitive color dramaturgy
limitations: Color-pair studies use constrained stimuli and cannot prescribe whole-scene storytelling palettes.
Model-generated color statistics do not directly measure human emotional response to finished illustration.
Display calibration, adaptation, color-vision variation, genre literacy, and culture can change perception.
reuse_note: Build palettes from relative value, chroma, and contextual roles; a single hue must never be treated as a universal emotion code.

mechanisms.statement: Interpret color through its combination with subject matter, neighboring colors, lightness, chroma, and scene context rather than through a single hue label.
Never map one color to a universal emotion; any emotional hypothesis must name the relevant color combination and contextual evidence.
Separate palette harmony, palette preference, and narrative usefulness because measured harmony and liking are related but not identical judgments.
Give the focal subject a deliberate figure-ground lightness relationship before using hue or saturation as the primary separator.
Assign dominant, supporting, and accent roles by relative area, value, and chroma instead of distributing every attractive color equally.
Check large value masses in grayscale so the story remains legible when hue contrast weakens across displays or viewers.
Express a narrative beat through a relative palette change from the established scene baseline, not through a supposedly universal warm or cool emotion rule.
Reserve the highest chroma or strongest local color contrast for one causally meaningful event, object, or relationship cue.

illustration_evidence_definitions.dominant_value_mass: Two or three large value groups organize the image before local rendering detail.
illustration_evidence_definitions.focal_value_separation: The main subject has a deliberate lightness relationship to its immediate background.
illustration_evidence_definitions.palette_role_map: Each major color family has a defined dominant, supporting, accent, or neutral function.
illustration_evidence_definitions.accent_chroma_budget: The strongest chroma or local color contrast is limited to narratively relevant regions.
illustration_evidence_definitions.temperature_transition: Warm-cool relationships change relative to the established palette baseline across depth or event state.
illustration_evidence_definitions.context_color_interaction: Any proposed color effect includes subject, neighboring palette, value, chroma, and situational context.
illustration_evidence_definitions.grayscale_readability: The principal subject and action remain separable after chroma is removed.
illustration_evidence_definitions.single_color_emotion_guard: No runtime rule assigns a universal emotion, personality, morality, gender, ethnicity, or nationality to one color.

candidate_definitions.dominant_value_mass: Choose two or three large value families before local color detail.
candidate_definitions.focal_value_separation: Specify a focal figure-ground lightness relation that survives desaturation.
candidate_definitions.palette_role_map: Declare dominant, supporting, accent, and neutral palette roles by area and function.
candidate_definitions.accent_chroma_budget: Spend the strongest chroma or color contrast on one meaningful cue.
candidate_definitions.temperature_transition: Describe warm-cool change only relative to the scene's established baseline.
candidate_definitions.context_color_interaction: Bind every color interpretation to subject, neighbors, value, chroma, and situation.
candidate_definitions.grayscale_readability: Require the core action and subject to pass a grayscale thumbnail check.
candidate_definitions.single_color_emotion_guard: Reject any prompt atom that treats one color as a universal human meaning.

compatibility: Combines with focal routing when the primary anchor owns the clearest value or chroma separation.
Combines with single-frame narrative when a palette transition marks a visible state change.
Combines with environmental depth through controlled value compression and relative temperature shifts.
Combines with motif systems when a recurring color changes role rather than carrying a fixed emotion.
Combines with crop resilience when palette roles survive reduced area and alternate aspect ratios.
conflicts: Conflicts with one-color-equals-one-emotion lookup tables.
Conflicts with equal saturation and equal local contrast across all regions.
Conflicts with a hue-only focal strategy that collapses in grayscale or varied color vision.
Conflicts with decorative rainbow accumulation unrelated to story or hierarchy.
Conflicts with palette changes that contradict the established lighting and material context.
counterexamples: A prompt that declares one hue universally angry, innocent, feminine, villainous, or national.
A scene whose subject disappears when converted to grayscale.
A limited palette where every small prop receives the maximum accent chroma.
A warm-to-cool shift claimed to communicate a fixed emotion without a scene baseline.
A harmonious color pair treated as proof that viewers will prefer or understand the image.
boundaries: A single color must never be encoded as a universal emotion, personality, morality, gender, ethnicity, or nationality.
Color-emotion findings are hypotheses conditioned on theme, neighboring colors, value, chroma, task, and culture.
Do not use palette associations to diagnose viewers or characters.
Do not copy a protected work's distinctive palette sequence or signature color arrangement.
Do not claim color accessibility without checking value contrast and relevant color-vision conditions.
format_implications: For thumbnails, preserve two or three large value masses and one accent.
For covers, include title-safe space in the value and palette-role map.
For cards, test the art both inside and outside its frame treatment.
For sequential or campaign art, define palette transitions relative to the prior image rather than as isolated labels.
viewer_implications: Viewers should locate the principal subject even with reduced chroma.
Color should reinforce context and hierarchy without dictating a single emotional reading.
A restrained accent should reward attention because it corresponds to a meaningful event or object.
Palette interpretation should remain open to individual and cultural variation.

title: Text-to-image models reveal specific color-emotion associations
supported_dimensions: Joint color features and combinations carried more information than simple one-hue associations.
The same hue can participate in different affective associations depending on context and chroma.
The study explicitly argues beyond simplistic mappings such as one color to one emotion.
limitations: The evidence comes from associations learned and rendered by text-to-image models, not direct ratings of the generated images by a representative human audience.
Training-data biases and prompt wording can influence observed color distributions.
The results do not justify universal emotion rules for a hue, culture, or person.
reuse_note: Use only the context-and-combination principle; preserve an explicit guard against universal single-color emotion mappings.

title: Aesthetic response to color combinations: preference, harmony, and similarity
supported_dimensions: Pair preference, pair harmony, and figural-color preference are distinct judgments.
Hue similarity, component preferences, and lightness relationships jointly affected ratings.
Formal color training and individual differences changed the relationship between harmony and preference.
limitations: Flat figure-ground color pairs do not capture complex illumination, materials, or narrative subject matter.
The participant population and calibrated laboratory display limit cultural and device generalization.
Average preference patterns do not prescribe a correct palette for an individual artwork.
reuse_note: Abstract relative hue, lightness, and role relationships; never convert population averages into universal emotional or demographic meanings.
